extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters and fiction writers (screenplays and films)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing story structure and setting for screenplays/films, covering avoidance of cliché, the four dimensions of setting, research methods, creative limitation, choice/pruning, and genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity — write only what you believe
rubrics_metrics.description: Write only what you believe; avoid making eccentric choices merely to avoid commercialism or to appear literary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preten tiousness (contrived rebellion against Hollywood/commercial norms) poisons work. Difference for the sake of difference is 'delinquency calling for attention.' If you work with 'one eye on your script and the other on Hollywood,' you risk producing an emotional temper tantrum rather than authentic art. The antidote is to commit to what you truly believe and let that conviction guide choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: War on cliché — know the world of your story
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliché stems from the writer's lack of genuine knowledge of the fictional world; writers crib scenes, dialogue, and characters from other works when they don't know their setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences are story-saturated and will spot reheated material. Originality and excellence require in-depth understanding and insight into your story's setting. If you lack knowledge of your fictional world you will default to familiar images from films/TV/novels and produce boring, obvious outcomes. Research and immersion in the world are keys to defeating cliché.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — four dimensions: Period, Duration, Location, Level of Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: A story's SETTING is four-dimensional: Period (place in time), Duration (length through time), Location (place in space), and Level of Conflict (social/human dimension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Period: contemporary, historical, future, or timeless/fantasy (examples: ANIMAL FARM, WATERSHIP DOWN). Duration: how much life-time the story spans (hours like MY DINNER WITH ANDRE; manipulations of time like LAST YEAR AT MARIENBAD; cinematic expansions like the 'Odessa Steps' sequence). Location: specific geography, buildings, rooms, planets, etc. Level of Conflict: where you pitch the story on the hierarchy of human struggles (inner/psychological, personal, institutional/political, environmental, etc.). The cast and their conflicts are part of the setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obey internal laws — consistency and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: A story must obey its own internal laws of probability; once you establish the causal principles of your fictional world, you cannot change them without violating the audience's contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each fictional world creates a unique cosmology and 'rules' for how things happen. If you break those rules (shifting causes, introducing coincidences that contradict established probability), the audience will feel violated and reject the story as illogical. Different genres tolerate different freedoms (fantasy demands tight internal logic; some gritty realism allows leaps sustained by style or device). Examples: strict Archplot in THE WIZARD OF OZ vs. THE USUAL SUSPECTS' law of free association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of creative limitation — create a small, knowable world
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the world of the story so a single artist can know it in depth; limitation inspires creativity rather than inhibiting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'small' world means knowable, not trivial. Great works focus narrowly (e.g., CRIME AND PUNISHMENT; DR. STRANGELOVE's limited sets and cast). The larger the world, the more diluted the writer's knowledge and the greater the risk of cliché; the smaller and better-known the world, the richer the creative choices. By the final draft, the writer should possess 'commanding knowledge' of all relevant details so no germane question about the world could not be answered instantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of setting — no portable story
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is not portable; specificity matters — place and time shape what can plausibly happen and how events read to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting choices constrain what events are possible or probable (e.g., a West L.A. gated estate won't plausibly riot; East L.A. housing projects won't plausibly hold thousand-dollar fundraisers). An 'honest story is at home in one, and only one, place and time.' Avoid vague or overly broad settings like 'America' when specificity would determine character behavior and event probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research — memory, imagination, and fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Win the war on cliché through research of memory, imagination, and fact: all three kinds are generally needed to build a saturated, believable world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memory: mine personal experience for sensory, emotional detail and relive and write it down (turn memory into working knowledge). Imagination: simulate living as your characters day-by-day; sketch routines and fragments to find hidden connections. Fact: go to the library and gather factual knowledge to expand your base of experience and generate insights. Research energizes talent, cures writer's block by giving you something to say, and often precipitates the moment characters 'come alive.' Warnings: research is not a substitute for creativity and must not become procrastination; it should feed invention and lead to the creation of events rather than merely accumulating information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity as choices — generate many variations and prune
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine writing requires inventing far more material than you use and making astute choices of inclusion and exclusion to find the small percentage of brilliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for ratios like five-to-one or ten-to-one (perhaps twenty-to-one). Sketch many alternative scenes (e.g., multiple ways lovers meet rather than trusting the first inspiratory idea). Then ask: which scene is truest to my characters, truest to their world, and has not been onscreen in quite this way before? Be willing to discard 90% of what you produce; genius includes the taste and will to weed out banalities, conceits, false notes, and lies. If a cliche proves to be the truest choice, exhaust its variations and research it until you can present it freshly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre knowledge and audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand genre and subgenre conventions because audiences bring sophisticated anticipations; you must fulfill and then lead those expectations to avoid confusion or boredom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genres can be classified by subject, setting, role, event, and values (examples and lists provided: Love Story, Horror with subgenres Uncanny/Supernatural/Super-Uncanny, Modern Epic, Western, War, Maturation Plot, Redemption Plot, etc.). The writer's knowledge of genre should surpass the audience's so he can satisfy necessary anticipations while delivering fresh, unexpected moments. Use genre knowledge to locate audience expectations and then subvert or deepen them responsibly.
